**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

There are about 30 trillion cells in your body, and every one of them is running a factory right now — without a manager, without instructions from you.

1. Read **The Factory You Are Made Of**. Each part has a JOB — that is the whole idea.
2. Learn the parts in the **Glossary**, then win the **Matching** game and the **Memory** game.
3. Study the **Job Chart** — it pairs each part with what it actually does.
4. Sort the cards in **Plant, Animal, or Both?** Careful: three of them fool people.
5. Take the quiz. It asks WHY, not just WHAT.
6. Fill in the **Cornell Notes** page in your own words — that page is your study sheet later.
7. Lock the ideas in with **Remember the Factory Floor** — study the example aid, then make one your own.
8. Finish with **Design Challenge: Build a Cell That Could Live Somewhere Else** — use what you learned on a real problem, and mark every guess as a guess.
9. Read the **The Factory Floor Plan** map by department before you take notes — structure fits function every time.

If you finish everything, you will be able to explain a cell without a diagram in front of you. That is the real goal. 🔬

Picture panels: Cell discoveries and plant structure; Animal cells and boundaries; Energy-processing organelles; Water and support. ## The Factory You Are Made Of

In 1665, Robert Hooke pointed a crude microscope at a thin slice of cork and saw tiny empty boxes. They reminded him of the small rooms monks lived in — *cells*. He was looking at the walls of dead plant cells, and he had no idea he had just named the basic unit of all life.

Every living thing is made of cells. Some organisms are a single cell; you are roughly 30 trillion of them. And a cell is not a bag of goo. It is a factory with departments.

The **cell membrane** is the security gate. It surrounds the cell and decides what enters and leaves — food and oxygen in, waste out. It is *selectively permeable*, which is a precise way of saying it lets some things through and blocks others.

The **nucleus** is the office where the instructions live. It holds DNA, the manual for building and running everything. Most of your cells carry a complete copy of that manual, even though a skin cell only ever reads the skin pages.

The **mitochondria** are the power plants. They take sugar and oxygen and release usable energy. Muscle cells, which need enormous energy, are packed with them.

The **cytoplasm** is the factory floor — the jelly-like fluid where the parts sit and most reactions happen. **Ribosomes** are the assembly machines that build proteins, the workhorses of the cell. The **endoplasmic reticulum** is the hallway system that moves those products around, and the **Golgi apparatus** is the shipping department: it packages proteins and labels them for delivery.

Plant cells have three parts animal cells lack. A rigid **cell wall** outside the membrane gives structure — it is why celery snaps and you do not. **Chloroplasts** capture sunlight for photosynthesis. And a large central **vacuole** stores water; when it is full the plant stands firm, and when it empties the plant wilts. That wilted houseplant is a storage problem, not a broken stem.

Here is what makes this worth memorizing: every one of those departments is running in you, right now, thirty trillion times over, with no supervision. Structure fits function at every level of biology, and the cell is where that pattern starts.
to:
## The Factory You Are Made Of

A microscope can turn a tiny patch of tissue into a landscape. Robert Hooke described boxlike compartments in cork in 1665 and called them cells. He saw walls left by dead plant cells, not all the working parts of a living cell.

Cells are the basic units of living organisms. Adult human bodies contain tens of trillions, with the number depending on the person. This lesson compares typical animal cells and photosynthetic plant cells. Bacteria have a different organization, and specialized cells do not all contain the same parts.

Think of a cell as a factory, but remember that the parts do not think or make plans. The **cell membrane** is a selective boundary: its lipids and proteins affect what crosses. Movement depends on molecular properties, concentration differences and transport proteins; some transport requires energy.

The **nucleus** contains most of a typical plant or animal cell's DNA. Cells use different combinations of genes, including many shared ones. Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own DNA. Some specialized cells, such as mature human red blood cells, lack a nucleus.

**Mitochondria** carry out major stages of aerobic cellular respiration. Energy from food molecules is transferred into ATP, which powers cellular work. Energy is transformed, not created. Plant cells also have mitochondria. Some steps of breaking down glucose occur in the cytosol outside mitochondria.

The **cytoplasm** includes the cytosol, a watery gel, and structures outside the nucleus. **Ribosomes** join amino acids to make proteins. Many proteins destined for secretion or membranes are made at the rough **endoplasmic reticulum**, where processing begins. Smooth ER has other roles, including lipid production. Transport vesicles carry materials to the **Golgi apparatus**, which modifies and sorts many proteins for delivery. Not every protein follows this route.

A typical photosynthetic plant cell has a **cell wall** outside its membrane, **chloroplasts**, and a large central **vacuole**. The wall provides support; chloroplasts use light energy in photosynthesis; the vacuole stores water and other materials. Many plant cells, including onion bulb cells, lack chloroplasts. Animals lack cell walls and chloroplasts, but both groups have membrane-bound transport compartments.

Water entering plant cells can build **turgor pressure**, pressing the cell contents against the wall. Water loss can reduce this pressure and make leaves droop. Vacuoles need not empty completely, and wilting can have other causes.

Use the pictures to connect structures with functions. Compare an onion cell with a green leaf cell: what is shared, what differs, and what evidence would a microscope actually let you see?

to: A cell is like a factory: a selective boundary, DNA library, ATP supply and protein assembly and processing areas. ER is a processing area, not just a hallway. No part thinks or chooses.

from: Example: the membrane is a thin flexible barrier with openings, which fits its job of letting some things through while blocking others. Mitochondria have folded inner surfaces that give lots of room for energy-releasing reactions, which fits their job as power plants.
to: Membrane lipids form a selective barrier and transport proteins help particular substances cross. Mitochondrial inner-membrane folds provide area for proteins involved in ATP production. Shapes help functions but model colors and sizes are conventions.

from: Making food and using food are different steps. Chloroplasts make sugar; mitochondria release the energy stored in that sugar. A plant still has to use its food, so it needs mitochondria too.
to: Photosynthesis makes sugars using light energy; cellular respiration transfers food energy into ATP. Plant cells use mitochondria in major stages of aerobic respiration, just as animal cells do.

from: Plant-only parts
to: Typical photosynthetic plant features and exceptions

from: Each one carries the same DNA manual but only reads the pages it needs. A liver cell and a skin cell have identical instructions and follow different chapters.
to: Most human cells contain similar nuclear DNA but use different combinations of genes, including many shared genes. Specialized cells differ; mature human red blood cells have no nucleus. The total cell count varies between people.

from: No — and biologists argue about whether they are even alive. A virus is genetic material in a protein coat with no membrane, no organelles, and no ability to reproduce without hijacking a real cell.
to: Viruses are not cells. They contain genetic material inside a protein coat; some also have a lipid envelope. They depend on host cells to reproduce.

from: Cell walls. Plant cells have rigid walls that snap; animal cells have only flexible membranes, so meat tears instead of crunching.
to: Plant cell walls and turgor help make fresh celery crisp. Food texture also depends on tissues, preparation and water content; it is not a complete cell-type test.

from: What is the biggest single cell?
to: Can a single cell be large enough to see?

from: An unfertilized ostrich egg is usually the answer given — a single cell you could hold in both hands. Some nerve cells are longer (a giraffe's can run meters) but far thinner.
to: Cells differ greatly in size and shape. A bird egg contains a large egg cell, but its shell and egg white are not parts of that single cell. Long nerve cells and large egg cells illustrate different kinds of size.

from: Constantly. Gut lining cells last days; skin cells weeks; red blood cells about four months. Some brain cells you keep for life — which is a strange thought.
to: Replacement rates differ by tissue. Many lining and blood cells are replaced regularly, while some nerve cells can persist for decades. A whole body does not replace all its cells on one schedule.

from: Design a model of a single cell adapted to one demanding environment. Every change you make to a part must be explained by structure fits function, using the real organelles from the lesson.
to: Design a hypothetical eukaryotic cell model for one environment. Explain structure and function, identify tradeoffs, and mark guesses. A design proposal is not evidence that cells evolve parts because they need them.

from: A science museum wants a display of imagined single cells, each built for a different place: a hot spring, deep ocean darkness, a dry desert crust, a fast-moving stream. Each model must be built from real cell parts, changed only in size, number, or shape, with a card explaining why.
to: A museum wants hypothetical eukaryotic cell models for a shaded pond, a sunlit pond or moving freshwater. Use real cell parts and identify what your model cannot establish about survival.

from: The nucleus holds the DNA instructions.
to: A typical eukaryotic nucleus contains most cellular DNA.

from: Mitochondria release usable energy from sugar and oxygen; cells that need more energy have more of them.
to: Mitochondria transfer food energy into ATP; abundance varies with cell type and demands.

from: Plant cells have a rigid cell wall, chloroplasts for photosynthesis, and a large central vacuole that stores water.
to: A typical photosynthetic plant cell has a wall, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole; not all plant cells have chloroplasts.

from: Nothing is invented that a real cell part could not do
to: State what evidence would be needed to test each predicted advantage; more of an organelle is not automatically better.

from: Every one of those departments is running in you, right now, thirty trillion times over, with no supervision. Structure fits function at every level of biology, and the cell is where that pattern starts.
to: Typical cell structures work together. The factory analogy has limits, specialized cells vary, and structure can help explain function.
